brief.situation: You are the database engineer for Fennick Outdoor, a fictional retailer. The orders service runs on Cloud Run and uses Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL orders-db (Enterprise Plus, max_connections 800). A flash sale started at 10:00 and peaks at 11:00. Since 10:12 about one checkout in five fails with a database error.
handover: Each Cloud Run instance opens its own connection pool (DB_POOL_MAX=10) at start-up.
orders-db's maintenance window is Wednesdays at 02:00; the sale ends at 13:00.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows Cloud Run's instances, their connection pools and orders-db.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why the database refused connections, what you changed during the sale, and why a pooler is the lasting fix.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Multiplies instances by pool size and notices the idle connections.
parts.modelAnswer: Cloud Run had no maximum and scaled to 184 instances, each opening a pool of 10: 1,840 connections wanted against max_connections 800. pg_stat_activity showed about 712 of them idle.

parts.label: During the sale
parts.criteria: Relieves it without restarting the database.
parts.modelAnswer: Capped Cloud Run at 60 instances and the pool at 8, at most 480 connections, deployed as a new revision with no database restart. Raising max_connections or enabling the pooler now would both restart orders-db at the peak.

parts.label: Lasting fix
parts.criteria: Justifies the pooler with the workload's shape and schedules it in the window.
parts.modelAnswer: A front end that scales to hundreds of short-lived instances needs many client connections but few server connections; managed connection pooling in transaction mode provides that, so it is scheduled for Wednesday's 02:00 window, after which the cap can rise.

expertPath.text: Errors: 'too many clients'; Cloud Run: 184 instances, no maximum, pool 10; pg_stat_activity: 712 of 800 idle.
Cap at 60 instances and pool 8 in one revision; schedule managed connection pooling for 02:00 Wednesday.
num_backends about 470 and 5xx near zero before 11:00.

restartedMidSale.headline: The right idea at the wrong time
restartedMidSale.body: Raising max_connections and enabling the pooler both restart a Cloud SQL instance. During the sale, limit the demand from the application side; make database changes that restart it in the maintenance window.

peakFailed.headline: The peak hit a full database
peakFailed.body: Instances times pool size is the number to bring under max_connections. A maximum instance count and a smaller pool do that in one deploy.

relieved.headline: Good: relief now, the pooler in the window
relieved.body: You measured the demand before changing anything, cut it from the application side without a restart, confirmed the errors stopped, and justified the pooler with what the workload actually does.

gaps.headline: Held, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria show what was left: the measurement, the pooler in the maintenance window, or the check.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: The database refuses connections because Cloud Run scaled to 184 instances with a pool of 10 each, 1,840 wanted against max_connections 800, and pg_stat_activity shows most of them idle. During the sale, bring the demand under the limit from the application side: a maximum instance count and a smaller pool, deployed as a revision, with no database restart. Raising max_connections or enabling the pooler now would restart orders-db at the peak. The lasting fix is a pooler: a serverless front end needs many short client connections but few server connections, which is what managed connection pooling in transaction mode gives; schedule it for the maintenance window and raise the cap afterwards.
